name: n2
responses:
An off-ramp can prevent escalation, preserve lives, and create space for a durable settlement. Allowing the adversary to portray the outcome as a domestic “victory” may be politically uncomfortable, but it is usually less costly than prolonging a dangerous confrontation merely to control the narrative.

Narratives do matter for legitimacy and deterrence, so they should not be ignored. But they are instruments, not the ultimate objective. The policy priority should be the concrete security result—reducing the threat, protecting allies and civilians, and preserving future leverage—provided the off-ramp does not conceal unacceptable concessions or undermine deterrence.

I selected the second statement because perceptions of victory and defeat can have real strategic effects. An adversary that can portray coercion or aggression as successful may preserve domestic support, strengthen hardliners, undermine deterrence, and encourage similar behavior in the future. Allies and partners also draw conclusions from how a crisis ends.

That does not mean refusing every face-saving compromise. A useful off-ramp can allow the adversary to claim success rhetorically while still securing the important substantive objectives—such as ending aggression, restoring deterrence, or protecting an ally. The key point is that narratives should not be dismissed as irrelevant: they can shape future behavior and therefore form part of the outcome.
